description: One-person team led by Junsu Park, building Rimlight: a lunar south-pole landing site and date navigator for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge.
summary: Rimlight answers one question for a lunar south-pole landing site and date: when will the lander see the Sun (power) and the Earth (direct radio contact)? It traces each site's 360° skyline from NASA LOLA elevation data and places the JPL Horizons Sun and Earth positions on it, hour by hour, for landing dates in 2026–2030. Example: for a 14-day mission landing on 23 July 2027 at the centre of NASA's Mons Mouton candidate region, a 2 m solar panel would see on average 19% of the Sun's disc (its energy share); at the best-lit point 446 m away, 60%.
details:
What it does. Pick one of 31 south-pole sites (Artemis candidate regions, commercial and international landers, published high-illumination points; five other landing sites farther north, such as Apollo 11, are shown on a smooth Moon for contrast) and a landing date.
- A 360° skyline shows the Sun's and Earth's paths and counts down to sunset and Earthset.
- Hour-by-hour stripes show when some of the Sun is in view, when Earth is in view and when both are, with the longest night and longest comms gap.
- A whole-region map for each of NASA's nine current candidate regions (2027; one point every 1 km, every 2 km on the large Mons Mouton Plateau): click a point for the full analysis there.
- "Small moves" compares the listed point with the highest and the best-lit point within 500 m, at panel heights of 0, 2 and 10 m.
- "If the launch slips" scores every landing day over six months.
- A table compares up to four site and date scenarios.

Who it is for. Mission planners get a first screen of sites, dates, panel height and launch slips. Teachers and students see why the pole is hard: the Sun circles the horizon, and a peak can be lit while the Sun is below 0°. The public can watch the Sun and Earth move over the skyline where Artemis astronauts may land.

How it works. LOLA polar elevation grids (40 m near the pole, 240 m beyond) are traced every 0.5° of azimuth out to 300 km (every 1° for clicked points and region maps). JPL Horizons gives the Sun and Earth positions; the browser turns them into sky directions that match Horizons' own output within 0.006°.

How we checked it. Against photographs: LRO's Wide Angle Camera recorded how often each 100 m patch at 88–90°S was lit in 3,807 images (2010–11). At 300 random points, Rimlight run for the same dates differs from the camera by 1.9 percentage points on average, on par with the LOLA team's published illumination map (2.1); most of those points are rarely lit ground. In 24 dated photos, mostly of 88–90°S, Rimlight's lit-or-dark call was right 94% of the time (95% interval 93–95%), against 79% for always guessing the more common state; we chose the photos' brightness threshold after seeing them, and the three thresholds we tried give 91–94%. Most Artemis regions are farther out, at 85–88°S, so every south-pole site position was also checked against dated photos: at the 32 positions outside 88°S, Rimlight was right 90% of the time (87–92%; 471 readings in 54 photos), against 71% for always guessing each site's more common state. Ridge crests are the hard case. There the error is about 14 points for Rimlight and 22 for the published map, crests cannot be ranked against each other, and when a crest looked dark Rimlight had called it at least partly lit 38% of the time. So the app treats crest differences under 20 points as ties and leads with energy share; choosing the best-lit point by energy share instead of hours picks the same point at 28 of 31 sites.

Limitations. Comms means line of sight only, with no antenna or link budget. Region maps sample one point per square kilometre, which misses small peaks: at Mons Mouton the best region point sees some Sun 61% of the time, the best-lit point near the centre 82%. At the Mons Mouton best-lit point, all 7 photographed hours that Rimlight calls partly lit looked dark, so much of its 82% is grazing Sun; read the energy share. This is a hackathon prototype, not a NASA tool.

Tools. Python (numpy, scipy), plain HTML/CSS/JavaScript with no framework, Playwright and ffmpeg for the demo video. Code is MIT-licensed.

Project authorship and AI use. I developed the project idea, solution approach and feature plan, and handled the organisers' requirements. I used an AI coding agent (Anthropic Claude) for research support, code and tests, technical validation, drafting text and scripting the demo recording. The demo is a screen recording of the real app; it contains no AI-generated images, video frames or voice. Details are in the repository README.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI):
Yes. I used an AI coding agent (Anthropic Claude, run through a command-line coding agent with several sub-agents) as a development tool.

My contribution: I developed the project idea, defined how to solve the challenge and planned the app's features. I interpreted and handled the organisers' requirements and directed the project. This includes the horizon panorama, hour-by-hour mission stripes, nearby-site comparison, launch-slip scan and region maps. I also registered for the Ottawa event and decided to enter as a one-person team.

AI assistance:
- Research support: summarising reference materials, including the official rules, challenge resources and past winners, and locating data access paths (PDS LOLA DEMs, JPL Horizons API, PGDA illumination maps, LROC WAC products).
- Code: writing the Python data pipeline and web app (HTML/CSS/JavaScript), including the tests, to implement my project plan.
- Technical validation: writing and running comparison and sensitivity scripts (published LOLA illumination maps, LROC camera map and dated photos, terrain-resolution tests). The assistant chose the photo brightness threshold after seeing the photos; this is stated in the app.
- Review support: running simulated judge reviews and helping correct numbers and wording.
- Text and video: drafting and editing project text and scripting the 30-second demo recording, with captions whose numbers are read from the app. No AI-generated images, video frames or voice are used.

The app's computed numbers come from NASA data processed by the repository's code; published comparison values are attributed to their sources.

Code and data processing: https://github.com/Ketchio-dev/rimlight

NASA Data:
- LRO LOLA Gridded Data Records, polar DEMs LDEM_85S_40M, LDEM_80S_40M, LDEM_75S_240M — PDS Geosciences Node — https://pds-geosciences.wustl.edu/lro/lro-l-lola-3-rdr-v1/lrolol_1xxx/data/lola_gdr/polar/img/
- JPL Horizons System (API) — https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/horizons/
- LOLA Lunar Polar Illumination maps, NASA GSFC PGDA product 69 — https://pgda.gsfc.nasa.gov/products/69
- LROC WAC south-pole illumination map WAC_POLE_ILL_TWI_SOUTH_100M and dated WAC polar frames (LROC RDR volume LROLRC_2001, PDS) — independent validation
- Used only in the validation experiments: LOLA polar DEMs ldem_85s_20m, ldem_875s_5m, ldem_75s_60m (same PDS directory); PGDA product 78 site coordinates (Barker et al. 2021).
